title: Cooking loss
summary: How much weight a preparation loses when it is cooked.

what: Cooking always reduces weight: first liquids, juices and fats evaporate, and with long cooking almost everything but the minerals. That loss is cooking loss.

Cooking loss changes with the type, method and equipment (boiling, frying, convection oven, griddle, grill…) and with the degree of doneness. Measuring it lets you choose, within good culinary practice, the method that loses the least.
formula: Weight before cooking = clean weight + inseparable additions
Loss = weight before cooking − cooked weight
Cooking loss % = loss ÷ weight before cooking × 100

variables.name: Clean weight
variables.description: The clean product, before cooking it.

variables.name: Inseparable additions
variables.description: Dressings, sauces, liquids, coatings or fillings that can't be separated afterwards.

variables.name: Cooked weight
variables.description: What the finished preparation weighs, ready to serve.

steps: Add the dressings, sauces, coatings or fillings that can't be separated.
Subtract the weights and work out the percentage on the weight before cooking.

examples.title: Marinated meat (illustrative)
paragraphs: Example: 1.200 kg of clean meat with 0.300 kg of marinade that can't be separated make 1.500 kg before cooking.
After cooking it weighs 1.050 kg: loss = 1.500 − 1.050 = 0.450 kg.

notes.text: The percentage is worked out on the weight before cooking (including additions), not on the gross weight you bought.
Besides cooking loss there's thawing loss (slowly freezing and thawing products that contain water) and drip loss (portioning too far in advance).
To avoid thawing loss, use a blast chiller, or buying fresh products more often and keeping them refrigerated at 4 °C.
